goals: Greet professionally and introduce yourself
Describe your skills with one concrete example
Ask one smart question at the end
scenarios.scene: You are interviewing for a junior data analyst internship at a software company. The interviewer is Ms. Ayesha. Be polite, confident, and specific.
scenarios.title: Job Interview

turns.coach: Smile, sit straight, greet first — first 10 seconds matter.
turns.say: Good morning! Thanks for coming in. Please, have a seat. So — tell me a little about yourself.

options.label: “Good morning. I'm Tanqeel, a data science student. I've built a sales dashboard in Python and I'm learning machine learning.”

notes.balanced: Strong — name, studies, and a concrete project. Interviewers remember specifics.
notes.soft: Great start — clear and confident.
notes.strict: Good. Upgrade: add one result — 'a sales dashboard that tracked…' What did it achieve?

options.label: “Hi, I'm Tanqeel. I study data science and I really need this job.”

notes.balanced: Honest, but 'I need this job' sounds desperate. Lead with what you OFFER, not what you need.
notes.soft: Good that you spoke up — now try leading with your skills.
notes.strict: Never say you 'need' the job. Flip it: what value do you bring them?

turns.prompt: Introduce yourself: name, studies, one concrete skill or project.

turns.coach: STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result. One short story beats ten adjectives.
turns.say: Nice. Tell me about a challenge you faced in a project — and how you handled it.

options.label: “In my dashboard project, the sales data was messy — missing dates everywhere. I wrote a Python script to clean it, and the final report was accurate.”

notes.balanced: Excellent STAR answer — problem, action, result. This is interview-ready.
notes.soft: Wonderful — a real story with a result.
notes.strict: Strong. To polish: add a number — 'cleaned 2,000 rows' hits harder.

options.label: “Umm… I haven't really faced challenges. Everything was fine.”

notes.balanced: This sounds like you have no experience. Every project has problems — pick a small one and tell it as a story.
notes.soft: Everyone faces challenges — even a small one makes a good story.
notes.strict: Weak answer. Interviewers read this as 'no real experience'. Always have one story ready.

turns.prompt: Describe a challenge using STAR: problem → your action → result.

turns.coach: Questions show interest. Never say 'no questions'.
turns.say: Good. We're almost done — do you have any questions for me?

options.label: “Yes — what does success look like in the first three months of this role?”

notes.balanced: Perfect closing question — shows you think like someone who wants to deliver.
notes.soft: Excellent question!
notes.strict: Perfect. Memorize this one — it works in almost every interview.

options.label: “No, I think everything is clear.”

notes.balanced: Missed opportunity. One smart question shows genuine interest — always prepare one.
notes.soft: It's okay to be nervous — but one question shows real interest.
notes.strict: This signals low interest. Always ask one prepared question.

turns.prompt: Ask one smart question. (Never say 'no questions.')

turns.say: Wonderful talking with you. We'll be in touch within a week. Have a great day!

goals: Check in with your booking details
Ask about Wi-Fi and breakfast politely
Handle a problem calmly if the room isn't ready
scenarios.scene: You arrive at a hotel in Islamabad after a long bus ride. Check in at the front desk.
scenarios.title: Hotel Check-in

turns.say: Good evening! Welcome to Pearl Continental. Do you have a reservation?

options.label: “Good evening. Yes, I have a reservation under the name Tanqeel.”

notes.balanced: Perfect — greeting + purpose + name. Exactly right.
notes.soft: Lovely and polite!
notes.strict: Flawless. Keep this exact pattern for every check-in.

options.label: “Room. I want room.”

notes.balanced: They'll understand, but it sounds rude. Add 'Good evening' and 'I have a reservation'.
notes.soft: They'll understand you — now let's make it polite.
notes.strict: Too blunt. In service situations, politeness IS the message.

turns.prompt: You booked online. Tell the receptionist.

turns.coach: Magic phrase: 'Could you tell me…?' — polite and natural.
turns.say: Yes, Mr. Tanqeel — one single room for two nights. Here's your key card. Anything else?

options.label: “Could you tell me the Wi-Fi password? And what time is breakfast?”

notes.balanced: Excellent — two polite questions in one turn. 'Could you tell me' is the magic phrase.
notes.soft: Great questions, very politely asked!
notes.strict: Textbook. This is how a confident traveller sounds.

options.label: “Wi-Fi password? Breakfast time?”

notes.balanced: Understood, but choppy. Full polite questions sound much better: 'Could you tell me…?'
notes.soft: Good questions — try them as full sentences.
notes.strict: Sounds like a telegram. Full sentences, please.

turns.prompt: Ask about Wi-Fi and breakfast.

turns.say: Of course — the Wi-Fi password is on the key sleeve, and breakfast is 7 to 10 in the lobby restaurant. Enjoy your stay!
Thank you! Have a wonderful evening, Mr. Tanqeel.

goals: Check in and drop your bag
Understand the gate and boarding time
Ask what to do about a delay
scenarios.scene: You are at Lahore airport, flying to Karachi. Your flight shows DELAYED on the board.
scenarios.title: At the Airport

turns.say: Hello! Passport and ticket, please. Are you checking in any bags?

options.label: “Hello. Here's my passport. Yes, one bag to check in, please.”

notes.balanced: Smooth and complete — greeting, documents, answer in one turn.
notes.soft: Very good — polite and clear!
notes.strict: Clean. This is exactly the rhythm of airport English.

options.label: “Yes, bag.” (hand over passport silently)

notes.balanced: Works, but silence feels cold. One greeting + one full sentence changes everything.
notes.soft: Good — now add a greeting and a full sentence.
notes.strict: Minimal answers at counters sound rude even when you don't mean it.

turns.prompt: Check in with one bag.

turns.say: All set — seat 14A, gate closes at 6:40. But I should warn you: the flight is delayed by about an hour.

options.label: “I see. Could you tell me the new boarding time, please?”

notes.balanced: Calm and smart — you accepted the news and asked the one useful question.
notes.soft: Very calm and polite — well handled!
notes.strict: Perfect delay handling: acknowledge, then ask for the key fact.

options.label: “Why delayed?! This is very bad!”

notes.balanced: The staff didn't cause the delay — anger won't speed up the plane. Stay calm, ask for facts.
notes.soft: Delays are frustrating — but calm questions get better answers.
notes.strict: Never shoot the messenger. Calm + factual always wins at airports.

turns.prompt: Your flight is delayed. Respond calmly.

turns.coach: 'Just to confirm' — the professional's safety net.
turns.say: New boarding time is around 7:45. Please stay near gate 4 and watch the screens.
You're welcome. Have a safe flight!

goals: Describe your symptoms clearly
Understand the doctor's instructions
Ask about medicine timing politely
scenarios.scene: You have had a fever and a sore throat for two days. You are at a clinic, talking to Dr. Sana.
scenarios.title: At the Doctor

turns.say: Hello, what seems to be the problem today?

options.label: “Hello, doctor. I have had a fever and a sore throat for two days.”

notes.balanced: Excellent — symptom + duration, using present perfect ('have had') like a native.
notes.soft: Very clear — the doctor knows exactly what's wrong!
notes.strict: Grammar point: 'I have had' (not 'I have') because it started in the past and continues. You nailed it.

options.label: “I am sick. Throat pain, fever.”

notes.balanced: The doctor will understand, but add duration: 'for two days' helps diagnosis a lot.
notes.soft: Good — now add 'for two days' and it's perfect.
notes.strict: Missing the most useful fact: how long. Always include duration.

turns.prompt: Describe your symptoms. Include how long.

turns.say: Let me check your throat… Yes, it's a throat infection. Nothing serious. I'll prescribe antibiotics — one tablet twice a day after meals, for five days.

options.label: “Just to confirm — one tablet twice a day after meals, for five days?”

notes.balanced: Perfect 'just to confirm' — repeating instructions back is what smart patients do.
notes.soft: Great — repeating it back shows you understood!
notes.strict: This is the professional move: repeat critical instructions back. Well done.

options.label: “Okay.” (nod silently)

notes.balanced: Risky — medicine instructions matter. Repeat them back: 'Just to confirm…'
notes.soft: It's okay to ask — repeating the instructions keeps you safe.
notes.strict: Never just nod at medical instructions. Repeat them back, every time.

turns.prompt: Make sure you understood the medicine instructions.

turns.coach: 'Should I avoid anything?' — the question most patients forget.
turns.say: Exactly right. Drink lots of water and rest. Come back if the fever stays after three days.
Get well soon! Next patient, please.

goals: Open the call warmly and state your purpose
Ask discovery questions about their needs
Close with a clear next step
scenarios.scene: Discovery call with a potential client, Mr. James from a UK retail company. He wants a sales dashboard. You have 15 minutes.
scenarios.title: Client Discovery Call

turns.say: Hi there! Thanks for jumping on. So — tell me, what are you hoping this dashboard will do for you?

options.label: “Hi James, thanks for your time. Before I explain anything, could you tell me how you track sales right now?”

notes.balanced: Brilliant — you asked before pitching. Discovery first, solutions later.
notes.soft: Lovely — asking first is exactly right!
notes.strict: This is how pros open: question before pitch. Memorize this move.

options.label: “Hi. I can build dashboards in Python with charts and everything. It's very good.”

notes.balanced: Pitching before understanding is the classic beginner mistake. Ask about THEIR world first.
notes.soft: Good energy — now aim it at his needs first.
notes.strict: Feature-dumping before discovery kills deals. Questions first, always.

turns.prompt: Open the call. (Hint: ask before you tell.)

turns.coach: Budget and timeline questions feel bold — that's why they work.
turns.say: Right now it's all Excel sheets, honestly. Takes my team hours every Monday. What would you need from me to get started?

options.label: “That Monday pain is exactly what I fix. Could you tell me your timeline — and is there a budget range in mind?”

notes.balanced: You mirrored his pain, then asked the two money questions politely. Textbook discovery.
notes.soft: Wonderful — you understood his problem and asked smart questions!
notes.strict: 'Could you tell me your timeline' + budget — the two questions juniors are afraid to ask. Well done.

options.label: “Okay, I can start tomorrow. It will take one week.”

notes.balanced: Too fast — you don't know the scope yet! Ask timeline and budget before promising anything.
notes.soft: Careful — promising speed before knowing the work is risky.
notes.strict: Never commit to timeline without scope. Ask first.

turns.prompt: He mentioned Excel pain. Dig deeper — timeline and budget.

turns.say: We'd like it live before the holiday season — so about two months. Budget is flexible for the right result.

options.label: “Two months works. I'll send you a short proposal with milestones by Friday — does that sound good?”

notes.balanced: Perfect close — summarized, proposed a concrete next step, and checked agreement.
notes.soft: Excellent closing — clear next step!
notes.strict: Close like this every time: recap + concrete next step + confirm.

options.label: “Okay great, I'll message you sometime.”

notes.balanced: Vague endings kill momentum. Always close with WHAT you'll send and WHEN.
notes.soft: Good — now make the next step concrete: what and when.
notes.strict: 'Sometime' is how deals die. What + when, every close.

turns.prompt: Close the call with a clear next step.

turns.say: Sounds good — proposal by Friday. Looking forward to it. Bye for now!

goals: Give a clear 30-second status update
Ask for help without sounding helpless
Disagree politely with a colleague's idea
scenarios.scene: Monday standup at your internship. Your manager Ali and teammate Sara are on the call. Give your update.
scenarios.title: Team Standup Meeting

turns.say: Morning, team! Quick round of updates. Tanqeel — what did you work on last week?

options.label: “Morning! Last week I cleaned the sales dataset and built the first dashboard draft. This week I'll add the monthly comparison charts.”

notes.balanced: Perfect standup format: done → next. Under 30 seconds, all signal.
notes.soft: Clear and confident — great update!
notes.strict: This is the done→next formula. Use it in every standup forever.

options.label: “Umm, I did some work on data… it was difficult… still working on it.”

notes.balanced: Vague updates worry managers. Name the task, name the result, name what's next.
notes.soft: Good effort — now make it concrete: what exactly did you finish?
notes.strict: Vague = invisible work. Done → next, with nouns.

turns.prompt: Give your update: done last week → plan this week.

turns.coach: 'I'm stuck on X, I've tried Y' — asking for help like a pro.
turns.say: Good progress. Anything blocking you?

options.label: “Yes — I'm stuck on the date formats in the old Excel files. I tried two approaches; could someone spare 15 minutes to look at it with me?”

notes.balanced: Pro-level ask: named the blocker, showed effort, made a small specific request.
notes.soft: Brave and smart — asking like this gets help fast!
notes.strict: This is the formula: blocker + what you tried + tiny specific ask.

options.label: “No, everything is fine.” (but you're stuck)

notes.balanced: Hiding blockers is the costliest habit in teamwork. Asking early is strength, not weakness.
notes.soft: It's okay to be stuck — the team is there to help.
notes.strict: Suffering silently burns days. Flag blockers within 24 hours.

turns.prompt: You're stuck on date formats. Ask for help properly.

turns.say: Sara, can you help Tanqeel after the call? Also — Sara, you suggested we skip the monthly charts. Thoughts, Tanqeel?

options.label: “I see Sara's point about saving time. But the client asked for monthly trends twice — could we do a simple version first?”

notes.balanced: Masterful disagreement: acknowledged her, cited the client, proposed a compromise.
notes.soft: Polite and smart — you disagreed without any friction!
notes.strict: 'I see your point, but…' + evidence + compromise. This is senior-level communication.

options.label: “No, that's wrong. We need the charts.”

notes.balanced: Direct contradiction creates enemies. Try: acknowledge → evidence → compromise.
notes.soft: You might be right — but the wrapping matters as much as the point.
notes.strict: Blunt 'no' in meetings costs you allies. Always cushion disagreement.

turns.prompt: Disagree with Sara politely. Use evidence.

turns.say: Good discussion. Sara, help Tanqeel with the dates after this. Back to work, team!

goals: Order food and drinks politely
Handle a wrong order without anger
Ask for the bill correctly
scenarios.scene: You are at a restaurant in Multan with a friend. The waiter comes to take your order.
scenarios.title: At the Restaurant

turns.say: Good evening! Welcome. Can I get you something to drink first?

options.label: “Good evening! Could I have a fresh orange juice, please?”

notes.balanced: Perfect — 'Could I have… please?' is the golden ordering phrase.
notes.soft: Lovely and polite!
notes.strict: 'Could I have X, please' — memorize this skeleton for all ordering.

options.label: “One juice.”

notes.balanced: Understood, but abrupt. 'Could I have…, please?' costs nothing and changes everything.
notes.soft: Good — now dress it up: 'Could I have…, please?'
notes.strict: Service staff remember politeness. Full phrase, always.

turns.prompt: Order a drink politely.

turns.coach: 'I'll have…' = the natural way to order food.
turns.say: One fresh orange juice — coming up. Are you ready to order food?

options.label: “Yes — I'll have the chicken karahi and two naans, please.”

notes.balanced: 'I'll have…' — natural, confident ordering. Well done.
notes.soft: Great ordering!
notes.strict: 'I'll have' beats 'I want' every time. Keep it.

options.label: “Give me chicken karahi.”

notes.balanced: 'Give me' sounds like a command. 'I'll have…' or 'Could I have…' instead.
notes.soft: Almost — try 'I'll have…' instead of 'give me'.
notes.strict: 'Give me' to waiters is a red flag. Never use it.

turns.prompt: Order your main dish.

turns.say: Here's your… oh no, I'm sorry! This is chicken handi — you ordered karahi. My mistake!

options.label: “No problem at all. Could you please change it when you get a chance?”

notes.balanced: Grace under pressure — you were kind AND clear about what you want. Staff love this.
notes.soft: So calm and kind — perfect handling!
notes.strict: This is emotional intelligence: forgive instantly, state the fix clearly.

options.label: “This is wrong! I said karahi! Take it back!”

notes.balanced: Mistakes happen — anger makes the meal worse for everyone, including you.
notes.soft: It's frustrating — but calm words fix it faster.
notes.strict: Never punish service staff for honest mistakes. Calm correction only.

turns.prompt: The order is wrong. Handle it with grace.

turns.say: Thank you for being so understanding! Your karahi is on its way — on the house dessert for the trouble.

goals: Answer Part 1 questions with 2-3 sentences
Speak for 2 minutes on the cue card
Discuss abstract ideas in Part 3
scenarios.scene: IELTS Speaking mock test with an examiner. Three parts: interview, long turn (cue card), discussion. Aim for Band 7+.
scenarios.title: IELTS Speaking Mock

turns.coach: Part 1: 2–3 sentences. Never one word, never a paragraph.
turns.say: Let's begin. Do you work or are you a student?

options.label: “I'm a data science student at Emerson University in Multan. I'm in my fifth semester and really enjoying the programming side.”

notes.balanced: Ideal Part 1 length — direct answer + one natural extension.
notes.soft: Great answer — just the right length!
notes.strict: Band 7 habit: answer + extend, then stop. You did exactly that.

options.label: “Student.”

notes.balanced: One word = Band 5 territory. Always extend: where, what, and one extra detail.
notes.soft: True — but give the examiner more to work with!
notes.strict: One-word answers cap your band. Extend every answer.

turns.prompt: Answer, then extend with one detail.

turns.say: Good. Now — describe a skill you would like to learn. You have one minute to prepare, then speak for two minutes.

options.label: “I'd like to master public speaking. First, because in my future career I'll present data to clients… Also, I admire speakers who make complex ideas simple. I've started by… ” (2-minute structured talk)

notes.balanced: Structured long turn — clear points, linking words, personal examples. That's Band 7+ shape.
notes.soft: Wonderful — organized and personal!
notes.strict: Note the skeleton: what → why → example → now. Use it for every cue card.

options.label: “I want to learn… um… cooking? Because… it's… useful. Yeah.”

notes.balanced: No structure, no development — this is where bands are lost. Pick the topic, then what/why/example.
notes.soft: It's okay to be nervous — structure is your safety net.
notes.strict: Cue cards punish hesitation. Memorize the what→why→example skeleton.

turns.prompt: Give a 2-minute structured talk: what → why → example.

turns.coach: Part 3: opinions + reasons + examples. Abstract thinking.
turns.say: Interesting. Let's discuss more broadly — do you think traditional skills are disappearing because of technology?

options.label: “To some extent, yes. For example, handwriting is declining as typing takes over. However, I believe technology also creates new skills — like data analysis — so it's more of a shift than a loss.”

notes.balanced: Balanced argument with concession ('however') and example — exactly what Part 3 rewards.
notes.soft: Thoughtful and balanced — excellent!
notes.strict: 'To some extent' + example + 'however' — this contrast structure is Band 7+ grammar in action.

options.label: “Yes, technology is bad for skills. People are lazy now.”

notes.balanced: Too absolute and too thin. Qualify ('to some extent'), give an example, show the other side.
notes.soft: A strong opinion is good — now support it with reasons and balance.
notes.strict: Absolute statements + no examples = Band 5. Qualify, exemplify, contrast.

turns.prompt: Give a balanced opinion with reasons.

turns.say: Thank you. That is the end of the speaking test.
